screens.title: Deployment sequence: why order matters
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying a sharded cluster is an ordered process because each component depends on metadata or connectivity provided by earlier components. The clean sequence is: first bring up and initialize the Config Server replica set, because mongos routers read cluster metadata from the config servers. Second, start each shard as a replica set so they can accept data. Third, start one or more mongos routers configured with the --configdb string that points to the initialized config replica set. Fourth, register each shard with the cluster using sh. addShard on a mongos. Finally, enable sharding for a database and shard a specific collection with sh. shardCollection. For a concrete example, plan three config members csReplSet on ports 27019–27021, two single-member shards shardA:27017 and shardB:27018 for testing, and a mongos on 27016. A common misconception is assuming mongos can start and operate without the config servers; in fact, mongos needs the config replica set to retrieve cluster metadata and will fail or behave incorrectly if the config servers are absent or not initialized. Key checks at each step are process reachability, rs. status for replica sets, and sh. status after adding shards. If you verify each step before moving on you avoid race conditions and ensure a reproducible deployment.

keyIdea.title: Sequential dependency
keyIdea.text: Config Servers → Shard Replica Sets → Mongos → Add Shards → Enable and shard collections.

content.html:
Core Concept › Deployment sequence
Why order matters
Each component requires metadata or registration from the previous step; skipping steps breaks routing or metadata consistency.
Step-by-step
  1. 1. Start and initiate Config Server replica set (csReplSet).
  2. 2. Start shard replica sets (shardA, shardB) with --shardsvr and replSet names.
  3. 3. Start mongos with --configdb pointing to the config replica set.
  4. 4. Connect to mongos and run sh.addShard(...) for each shard.
  5. 5. Enable database sharding and shard collections with sh.shardCollection(...).
Example local plan
csReplSet: localhost:27019,27020,27021 · shardA: localhost:27017 · shardB: localhost:27018 · mongos: localhost:27016
Common misconception
Some try to start mongos before config servers are initialized. Mongos requires an initialized config replica set to retrieve cluster metadata and will not function properly without it.
Checklist while you deploy
  • Verify process on expected port and host after startup.
  • Run rs.initiate and confirm rs.status returns a PRIMARY for each replica set.
  • Start mongos with the exact --configdb string including replSet name and hosts.
  • After sh.addShard run sh.status to confirm registration.
Key Takeaway
Follow the sequence, verify status after each step, and avoid starting mongos until config servers are healthy.

screens.title: Config Servers as a replica set
screens.narratorSegment: Config Servers hold the cluster’s metadata: chunk ranges, shard mappings, and the cluster topology that mongos routers use to route queries and writes. In a sharded cluster the config servers must run as a replica set to ensure high availability and consistent metadata. For a basic local setup, create three data directories, start three mongod instances with the --configsvr flag, the same --replSet name, and distinct ports. Then connect to one member and run rs. initiate with a configsvr true flag and a members array listing each host and port. After initiation, rs. status shows the replica set health. A concrete startup example uses ports 27019, 27020, and 27021. A common mistake is to forget the configsvr: true field or to pass inconsistent replSet names between the mongod startup flags and rs. initiate; both will cause mongos to fail when it tries to read the configdb. Remember: if your config servers are not a healthy replica set, mongos cannot obtain the cluster metadata necessary to route requests. Check the replica set state before proceeding to start mongos. Config Servers as a replica set means config servers must be configured as a replica set and initialized before starting mongos so metadata is available.. In practical terms, what config servers store and why they must be initialized first. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Config servers first
keyIdea.text: Config Servers must be configured as a replica set and initialized before starting mongos so metadata is available.

content.html:
Definition › Config Servers
Config Servers store cluster metadata
Initialize as a replica set to provide consistent metadata to mongos routers.
Example startup commands
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb1 --port 27019 --bind_ip localhost
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb2 --port 27020 --bind_ip localhost
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb3 --port 27021 --bind_ip localhost
Replica set initiation
rs.initiate({
  _id: "csReplSet",
  configsvr: true,
  members: [
    { _id: 0, host: "localhost:27019" },
    { _id: 1, host: "localhost:27020" },
    { _id: 2, host: "localhost:27021" }
  ]
})
Supporting notes
  • Config servers are authoritative for chunk metadata and must be highly available.
  • Use at least three config server members in production to protect from split-brain.
  • Always match the --replSet name in mongod startup flags and the rs.initiate configuration.
Common mistake
Starting mongos before config replica set is initialized or using conflicting replSet names.
Key Takeaway
Config servers must be a healthy replica set and verified with rs.status before starting mongos.

keyIdea.title: Terminal steps matter
keyIdea.text: Start each config mongod with the correct flags, initiate the set with configsvr: true, and verify with rs.status.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Init Config Servers
Start config server processes
Create directories and run these startup commands in separate terminals or background processes.
# Config Server 1
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb1 --port 27019 --bind_ip localhost

# Config Server 2
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb2 --port 27020 --bind_ip localhost

# Config Server 3
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb3 --port 27021 --bind_ip localhost
Initiate replica set in the mongo shell
rs.initiate({
  _id: "csReplSet",
  configsvr: true,
  members: [
    { _id: 0, host: "localhost:27019" },
    { _id: 1, host: "localhost:27020" },
    { _id: 2, host: "localhost:27021" }
  ]
})

# Verify
rs.status()
Example verification
rs.status should show one PRIMARY and two SECONDARYs. If not, check logs and replSet name consistency.
Common mistake
Forgetting configsvr: true or using a different replSet name in rs.initiate than the mongod --replSet flag.
Key Takeaway

Start the config servers, initiate the replica set with configsvr: true, and only then proceed to shard startup and mongos.

screens.title: Deploy shard replica sets
screens.narratorSegment: Each shard should be a replica set to provide data redundancy and availability. In a test environment you may run a single member per shard for simplicity, but in production use at least three members per shard. Begin by creating data directories for each shard member and starting mongod with the --shardsvr flag and the same --replSet name for all members of that shard. For example, start shardA's primary on port 27017 with --shardsvr and --replSet shardA. After the process is running, connect to its mongo shell and run rs. initiate with the shard's _id equal to the replSet name and a members array listing the member hosts. A concrete example: start shardA on localhost:27017 and shardB on localhost:27018, each initiated as their respective replica sets. Verify each with rs. status. A misconception is treating shard mongod instances like simple standalone servers; they must be started with --shardsvr and joined to a replica set so the cluster can move chunks and maintain consistent data. Verify replication health before adding shards to mongos. Deploy shard replica sets means start shard mongod instances with --shardsvr and initiate each as a replica set before registering them with mongos.. In practical terms, start shard nodes with --shardsvr and initialize their replica sets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Shards as replica sets
keyIdea.text: Start shard mongod instances with --shardsvr and initiate each as a replica set before registering them with mongos.

content.html:
Process Flow › Shard Replica Sets
Start shard mongod instances
Each shard must be a replica set. Use --shardsvr and a shared replSet name per shard.
# Shard A member
mongod --shardsvr --replSet shardA --dbpath /data/sharda1 --port 27017 --bind_ip localhost

# Shard B member
mongod --shardsvr --replSet shardB --dbpath /data/shardb1 --port 27018 --bind_ip localhost
Initiate shard replica set
rs.initiate({
  _id: "shardA",
  members: [ { _id: 0, host: "localhost:27017" } ]
})

# Repeat for shardB on port 27018
Notes and checks
  • Even single-member shards for testing need --shardsvr flag to be recognized as shard members.
  • In production, run at least three members per shard for failover and to support elections.
  • Verify each shard with rs.status and confirm primary selection before adding to mongos.
Key Takeaway
Shards must be replica sets and started with --shardsvr so the cluster can perform balancing and replication correctly.

screens.title: Start mongos routers
screens.narratorSegment: With config servers and shards initialized, the next step is to start mongos routers. Mongos does not store data; it routes queries using the metadata from the config replica set. When starting mongos you must pass the --configdb option with the config replica set name followed by the host:port list, for example csReplSet/localhost:27019,localhost:27020,localhost:27021. Choose a port for mongos that does not conflict with shard ports; a common test port is 27016. After mongos starts, connect to it with the mongo shell and run sh. status to inspect cluster state. A common mistake is using a --configdb string that references standalone mongod instances or incorrect hostnames — mongos expects a config replica set. If mongos can’t connect to the config servers or the config replica set is not initialized, it will fail to provide routing information. For production, run multiple mongos instances to avoid a single router becoming a bottleneck. As a final check, ensure you can connect to mongos and that sh. status lists the expected shards. Start mongos routers means start mongos with --configdb using the config replica set name and hosts so it can retrieve metadata and route queries.. In practical terms, how to point mongos at the config server replica set. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mongos requires configdb
keyIdea.text: Start mongos with --configdb using the config replica set name and hosts so it can retrieve metadata and route queries.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Start mongos
Starting mongos
Provide the config replica set in --configdb so mongos can access cluster metadata.
mongos --configdb csReplSet/localhost:27019,localhost:27020,localhost:27021 --port 27016 --bind_ip localhost
Verify mongos and cluster status
Connect to mongos and run sh.status() to confirm registered shards and routing table availability.
Troubleshooting tips
  • Check the --configdb string for exact replSet name and host:port entries.
  • Confirm config replica set is initialized and reachable from the mongos host.
  • Use multiple mongos instances in production for resilience and load distribution.
Key Takeaway
Mongos depends on the config replica set; start it only after config servers are healthy and reachable.

screens.title: Add shards to the cluster
screens.narratorSegment: After mongos is running and connected to the config servers, you must register each shard with the cluster using sh. addShard. Connect to the mongos shell and run sh. addShard with a string that identifies the shard's replica set name and at least one host:port for that set, for example sh. addShard("shardA/localhost:27017"). Repeat for each shard. Once added, run sh. status to confirm the shards appear in the cluster and that the cluster is aware of available shard servers. One common misconception is believing sh. addShard performs replication or initialization; it simply registers an already-initialized replica set as a shard. Therefore, ensure each shard replica set has been initiated and is healthy before adding it to mongos. Code Walkthrough › Add Shards
Register your shard replica sets
Use the mongos shell to add each shard so the cluster knows where to place data.
# From mongos shell
sh.addShard("shardA/localhost:27017")
sh.addShard("shardB/localhost:27018")

# Verify
sh.status()
Important note
sh.addShard registers an already-initialized replica set; it does not initialize replication or change the shard's internal configuration.
Troubleshooting
  • Check that the target host:port is reachable from mongos.
  • Ensure the shard mongod was started with --shardsvr and correct replSet name.

screens.title: Enable sharding and shard a collection
screens.narratorSegment: Once shards are registered, enabling sharding for a database and sharding specific collections are the final configuration steps. From the mongos shell run sh. enableSharding("mydatabase") to mark a database as sharded. Then choose an appropriate shard key and run sh. shardCollection with the full namespace and a key specification, for example sh. shardCollection("mydatabase. mycollection", { "_id": "hashed" }). A ranged key like { myShardKey: 1 } creates contiguous ranges; a hashed key spreads writes across shards but makes range-based queries less efficient. A common misconception is thinking enabling sharding automatically shards existing collections; you must run sh. shardCollection for each collection you want distributed. Also, choose shard keys carefully: a poor shard key can create hotspots and imbalance. After sh. shardCollection runs, MongoDB begins redistributing chunks based on the key, and new writes are routed to the correct shard. Verify distribution with sh. status and by inspecting chunk counts per shard. Enable sharding and shard a collection means enable sharding for a database, then shard each collection with a chosen shard key; hashed keys increase write distribution while ranged keys support range queries.. content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Enable & Shard
Enable sharding and shard collections
Use mongos to turn on sharding for a database and then shard chosen collections with a deliberate key.
# Enable sharding for the database
sh.enableSharding("mydatabase")

# Shard the collection (hashed key example)
sh.shardCollection("mydatabase.users", { "_id": "hashed" })

# Or a ranged key
sh.shardCollection("mydatabase.orders", { "orderDate": 1 })
Choosing a shard key
Hashed keys distribute writes but defeat range queries; ranged keys preserve range query performance but can cause hotspots if values are monotonic.
Checks after sharding
  • Confirm chunk creation and distribution with sh.status().
  • Monitor for chunk imbalances and consider balancer state.
  • Measure application query patterns to validate shard key choice.
Key Takeaway
Enable the database, shard each collection explicitly, and choose a shard key that balances distribution and query needs.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: Deployers commonly make a few recurring mistakes that prevent a sharded cluster from working. First, mismatched replica set names between the mongod --replSet flag and the rs. initiate payload will prevent members from joining and break cluster formation. Second, forgetting to include --configsvr for config servers or --shardsvr for shard nodes means mongod instances will not be recognized as the intended roles. Third, attempting to start mongos against standalone mongod instances rather than an initialized config replica set causes mongos to fail when it tries to read metadata. Another significant safety issue is using single-node replica sets in production: they remove failover and create single points of failure. Also remember network and firewall rules; components must be able to reach each other on the configured ports. Misconceptions to check: sh. addShard does not initialize replica sets, and enabling sharding does not automatically shard existing collections unless you run sh. shardCollection. Your practice on a local, simulated plan should exercise the exact order and verification commands to avoid these common traps. content.html:
Common Mistakes › Safety Notes
Compare mistake → effect
Know the symptom so you can quickly identify the root cause in logs and status checks.
Mismatched replSet names
Members refuse to join; replica set stays uninitialized and mongos cannot retrieve config metadata.
Missing --configsvr or --shardsvr
Nodes will not be treated as config servers or shard servers and registration will fail.
Single-node in production
No failover, single point of failure; avoid for any production deployment.
Quick remedies
  • Match replSet names exactly in startup flags and rs.initiate payloads.
  • Confirm each mongod started with the correct role flag and reachable ports.
  • Use at least three members for config and shard replica sets in production.
Practice tip
When an error occurs, check the mongod and mongos logs and verify rs.status and sh.status to pinpoint which component failed.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Local Setup Plan
Plan your local cluster
Translate the chapter example into a set of commands you can run in separate terminals or containers.
Suggested command list (write these down)
# Config servers
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb1 --port 27019 --bind_ip localhost
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb2 --port 27020 --bind_ip localhost
mongod --configsvr --replSet csReplSet --dbpath /data/configdb3 --port 27021 --bind_ip localhost

# Shard servers
mongod --shardsvr --replSet shardA --dbpath /data/sharda1 --port 27017 --bind_ip localhost
mongod --shardsvr --replSet shardB --dbpath /data/shardb1 --port 27018 --bind_ip localhost

# Mongos router
mongos --configdb csReplSet/localhost:27019,localhost:27020,localhost:27021 --port 27016 --bind_ip localhost
Configuration commands to run from shells
# Initiate config replica set (from one config server shell)
rs.initiate({...})

# Initiate each shard replica set (from its shell)
rs.initiate({...})

# From mongos shell
sh.addShard("shardA/localhost:27017")
sh.addShard("shardB/localhost:27018")
sh.enableSharding("myAppDB")
sh.shardCollection("myAppDB.users", {"_id": "hashed"})
Verification steps
  1. Run rs.status on each replica set and confirm PRIMARY selection.
  2. Start mongos and run sh.status to confirm shards are registered.
  3. After sh.shardCollection, inspect chunk distribution across shards.
Key Takeaway
Drafting and verifying commands locally prepares you to run the same steps on cloud VMs or containers reliably.

screens.title: Verification and common checks
screens.narratorSegment: Verification at every major step prevents cascading failures later. After starting config servers, run rs. status and confirm a PRIMARY and SECONDARYs. When starting shard replica sets, repeat rs. status for each shard and confirm it has an elected PRIMARY. After starting mongos, run sh. status to verify that mongos recognizes the config replica set and any added shards. After sh. addShard, check that the shard appears in sh. status and that the cluster has an expected number of shards. After sh. enableSharding and sh. shardCollection, confirm chunk creation and distribution: sh. status shows sharded collections and the chunk counts per shard. If any verification step fails, consult mongod and mongos logs for connection or replica set errors. A frequent cause of failures is network reachability or port conflicts; check that your bind_ip and ports are correct and that there are no firewall rules blocking traffic. The practical checklist: verify rs. status for every replica set, verify sh. status after shard registration, and inspect chunk distribution after sharding a collection. These checks give you confidence the cluster will route and distribute data correctly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the full, logical sequence for deploying a basic MongoDB sharded cluster. We’ll focus on why the order matters, the concrete mongod and mongos startup commands, the shell commands that wire the cluster together, and the common mistakes that stop a deployment from working. You will see how Config Servers hold cluster metadata, why they must be initialized first as a replica set, and how each shard must also be a replica set. You’ll also learn how to start a mongos router, add shards with the shell command, enable a database for sharding, and shard a collection with an appropriate shard key. As an example, we’ll use local ports and replica set names so you can map commands to a simulated lab. Keep in mind production requirements: Config Servers and Shards should be replica sets and you should run multiple mongos routers for resilience. By the end of this chapter you will be able to plan and write the startup commands, initialize replica sets, and execute the sh. addShard, sh. enableSharding and sh. shardCollection commands with confidence.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to plan and execute the steps required to bring up a basic sharded cluster. Objective one covers the ordered steps from config servers to shards to mongos routers, explaining why the sequence is essential for operational correctness. Objective two focuses on running the startup commands for mongod and mongos, including the required flags such as --configsvr, --shardsvr and --replSet, and how those flags change behavior. Objective three walks through the shell commands sh. addShard, sh. enableSharding and sh. shardCollection so you can configure sharding for a database and its collections. Objective four prepares you to recognize and resolve common deployment problems like mismatched replSet names, missing configsvr flags, or firewall port issues. Each objective pairs a clear skill with a practical reason why it matters, and a brief mnemonic so you can remember the correct ordering when you script a deployment.

This second objective slide expands the checklist into practical micro-skills you will use during deployment. You will practice writing the mongod startup lines for config servers and shards, and the mongos startup line that references the config server replica set. A useful skill is verifying replica set health with rs. status and confirming shards are registered with sh. status. We will also highlight the importance of consistent replSet names and flags; mismatches are a frequent source of failure during mongos startup. As you simulate the local plan, write the exact startup and configuration commands and perform a dry run in a terminal window. Finally, you will learn two safety checks: confirm network reachability on each port and avoid using single-node replica sets for production. These micro-skills turn the objectives into repeatable steps you can apply in a cloud VM, container, or local multi-process environment.

Deploying a sharded cluster is an ordered process because each component depends on metadata or connectivity provided by earlier components. The clean sequence is: first bring up and initialize the Config Server replica set, because mongos routers read cluster metadata from the config servers. Second, start each shard as a replica set so they can accept data. Third, start one or more mongos routers configured with the --configdb string that points to the initialized config replica set. Fourth, register each shard with the cluster using sh. addShard on a mongos. Finally, enable sharding for a database and shard a specific collection with sh. shardCollection. For a concrete example, plan three config members csReplSet on ports 27019–27021, two single-member shards shardA:27017 and shardB:27018 for testing, and a mongos on 27016. A common misconception is assuming mongos can start and operate without the config servers; in fact, mongos needs the config replica set to retrieve cluster metadata and will fail or behave incorrectly if the config servers are absent or not initialized. Key checks at each step are process reachability, rs. status for replica sets, and sh. status after adding shards. If you verify each step before moving on you avoid race conditions and ensure a reproducible deployment.

Config Servers hold the cluster’s metadata: chunk ranges, shard mappings, and the cluster topology that mongos routers use to route queries and writes. In a sharded cluster the config servers must run as a replica set to ensure high availability and consistent metadata. For a basic local setup, create three data directories, start three mongod instances with the --configsvr flag, the same --replSet name, and distinct ports. Then connect to one member and run rs. initiate with a configsvr true flag and a members array listing each host and port. After initiation, rs. status shows the replica set health. A concrete startup example uses ports 27019, 27020, and 27021. A common mistake is to forget the configsvr: true field or to pass inconsistent replSet names between the mongod startup flags and rs. initiate; both will cause mongos to fail when it tries to read the configdb. Remember: if your config servers are not a healthy replica set, mongos cannot obtain the cluster metadata necessary to route requests. Check the replica set state before proceeding to start mongos. Config Servers as a replica set means config servers must be configured as a replica set and initialized before starting mongos so metadata is available.. In practical terms, what config servers store and why they must be initialized first. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Once shards are registered, enabling sharding for a database and sharding specific collections are the final configuration steps. From the mongos shell run sh. enableSharding("mydatabase") to mark a database as sharded. Then choose an appropriate shard key and run sh. shardCollection with the full namespace and a key specification, for example sh. shardCollection("mydatabase. mycollection", { "_id": "hashed" }). A ranged key like { myShardKey: 1 } creates contiguous ranges; a hashed key spreads writes across shards but makes range-based queries less efficient. Deployers commonly make a few recurring mistakes that prevent a sharded cluster from working. First, mismatched replica set names between the mongod --replSet flag and the rs. initiate payload will prevent members from joining and break cluster formation. Second, forgetting to include --configsvr for config servers or --shardsvr for shard nodes means mongod instances will not be recognized as the intended roles. Third, attempting to start mongos against standalone mongod instances rather than an initialized config replica set causes mongos to fail when it tries to read metadata. Another significant safety issue is using single-node replica sets in production: they remove failover and create single points of failure. Also remember network and firewall rules; components must be able to reach each other on the configured ports. Misconceptions to check: sh. addShard does not initialize replica sets, and enabling sharding does not automatically shard existing collections unless you run sh. shardCollection.
